Well, like I was just saying, yeah... I guess afraid is the right word. If I see the scale go up even a tiny bit, like after one of those dinners or if I eat something with bread, I get really tense. I just have to start cutting back the very next day so it doesn't stick. 

Bread is just... it's so heavy. Actually, there's this artisanal bakery right next to the Victorian we're painting this week over on Elm Street. They start baking sourdough at like 4 AM, so by the time I'm out there setting up the scaffolding, the whole block just smells unbelievable. We're doing all the exterior trim on the house next door, and let me tell you, the owner picked this absolute nightmare of a color. It's this bright, mustard yellow. I tried to tell the guy, I said, "Look, buddy, this is gonna completely clash with your red brick," but he wouldn't listen. People just have zero eye for color these days. They see some trendy design on HGTV and think it's gonna work on a classic 1920s house. It’s ridiculous. Plus, yellow is notorious for terrible hide. I'm gonna have to put on three coats of the stuff just to get it to cover the old dark green paint. It's eating up my entire profit margin on labor alone. 

But yeah, anyway... I just get really anxious about the weight sticking if I eat stuff like that, so I make sure to fix it immediately the next day.

Well, yeah, I definitely avoid certain things. I mean, most days I really just keep it to coffee, maybe I'll grab a protein bar between paint jobs if I really need to, and then just a small dinner. Eating a full, heavy meal just... it feels like it would totally slow me down, you know?

Well, I'm still getting all my painting jobs done, so it's not really impacting my work itself. But I guess... I do avoid some client meals or, like, social plans with friends lately. I just really don't want the situation to turn into people commenting on what I eat or how I look, you know? It's just easier to bow out. 

Especially with clients, they always want to feed you when you're working inside their house. You have to use a tinted primer, usually a dark gray, and even then, you're looking at three coats minimum to get a solid, even finish without flashing. And if you don't keep a wet edge while you're rolling, you will see every single roller mark when the afternoon light hits it from the window. It took me three days just to do that one room because of the dry time between coats. 

But yeah, I just try to avoid eating with people so I don't have to deal with the comments. It just makes things simpler.

Controlling my life? No, I wouldn't go that far. I mean, I'm the one making my own choices. I've always liked being in control of things, honestly. You kind of have to be in my line of work.

Gained a little weight? No. No, man, absolutely not. If the scale goes up even a little bit, like if I do end up at a client dinner or eat something with bread, I get incredibly tense. 

Actually, a lot of those client dinners happen right in the middle of kitchen remodels. I just quoted a massive kitchen job yesterday. The homeowners want me to paint their old nineties honey oak cabinets white. And everybody watches those DIY shows and thinks you can just slap some latex paint over varnished oak with a foam roller. It's ridiculous. Oak has deep open grain, and the tannin bleed will come right through water-based paint in a week, turning it yellow. You have to scrub years of cooking grease off with TSP, sand every single contour of those doors, and then you have to spray a shellac-based primer. 

And let me tell you, spraying shellac is a completely different beast. You need an airless sprayer with a fine finish tip—like a 310 or 312—and because shellac dries so fast, if you stop for even five minutes, the tip clogs solid. Plus, the masking... oh man. It takes three full days just to mask a kitchen. You have to wrap the entire room in plastic, cover the floors in heavy Ram Board, tape off all the appliances... because if atomized shellac overspray lands on a custom granite countertop, you are basically buying them a new kitchen. You have to clean the whole rig out with ammonia or denatured alcohol afterward, too, you can't just run water or paint thinner through it. 

But, uh... anyway. What were we talking about? Oh, right. Gaining weight. Yeah, no, if I see that scale move up at all after eating something heavy, I just start cutting back the next day so it doesn't stick. I definitely wouldn't feel better about myself if I gained.

Yeah, it sneaks up on me a lot. Like... if I catch myself in a mirror, or especially in photos next to one of my murals. 

I do a lot of large-scale commercial murals for businesses around town, mostly on the sides of old buildings. And man, those exterior brick jobs are exhausting. People don't realize you can't just slap regular exterior latex on raw brick. The alkalinity in the masonry will literally burn the tint right out of the paint in six months. You have to pressure wash it first, let it dry completely, and then back-roll a heavy coat of masonry primer—something like Loxon—into every single mortar joint. You go through roller covers like crazy because the brick just shreds them. A three-quarter-inch nap is the bare minimum, and even then you're constantly jamming the brush in there to fill the pinholes. 

And getting the proportions right on a two-story wall is a whole other nightmare. I usually have to rent a tow-behind boom lift, wait until it's pitch black outside, and shine a high-lumen projector from across the street just to trace the outline. If you mess up the grid or the angle of the projector is off by even a few degrees, the whole image gets warped. 

So you put all this blood, sweat, and tears into it for weeks... and then the business owner comes out and wants to take a picture of you standing next to the finished piece for their social media. And honestly? When I look at those photos, or if I just catch my reflection in the storefront glass while I'm loading the lift back onto the trailer, I'm not even looking at the artwork I just spent weeks on. I basically judge the whole day by whether my stomach and face look sharp enough in that moment. It just completely takes over my head, even when I'm supposed to be celebrating a finished job.

If you don't use the brightener, the pH balance of the wood is totally out of whack from the stripper, and your new stain will look completely blotchy and probably fail within a year. Plus, you have to check the boards with a moisture meter and make sure it's reading below fifteen percent before you can even think about applying a penetrating oil stain. We actually had to pack up and wait three extra days on that job because it rained and the wood swelled up. \n\nBut anyway, yeah. Dave's cookout. I just skipped it. I'd rather just stay home than deal with the comments, you know? It's just easier to avoid it altogether.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your concerns about weight are interfering with your ability to enjoy your daily life?\n\nPatient: I feel like I'm a bit of a broken record here, but yeah, it's basically what I was saying before. My daily life is mostly work, and I'm still getting all my painting jobs done on time, so that part is fine. It's just... I avoid the client meals and the social plans because I really, really don't want to deal with people commenting on what I'm eating or how I look. It just ruins the enjoyment of the day, you know? \n\nLike, if I'm working on a historic home—which I do a lot of in the older neighborhoods downtown—the homeowners always want to come out and offer you sandwiches or sit on the porch with you. And those old houses, man, you have to be so incredibly careful. If the house was built before 1978, you're almost definitely dealing with lead paint. You can't just go out there and scrape it dry like a normal house. You have to follow strict EPA RRP rules—Renovation, Repair, and Painting. You have to lay down heavy six-mil plastic extending at least ten feet out from the foundation, tape it to the house, put up caution signs, and you have to wet-scrape everything so the lead dust doesn't become airborne or get into the soil. \n\nIf the EPA or OSHA catches you dry-scraping lead paint, the fines are absolutely astronomical. We're talking tens of thousands of dollars per violation. Plus, you have to wear a P100 half-mask respirator the entire time, and let me tell you, it gets so incredibly hot breathing inside that heavy rubber mask in the middle of July. You're sweating buckets, your safety glasses are fogging up. You have to wear a disposable Tyvek suit, too. \n\nSo the absolute last thing I want to do is go through the whole decontamination process, take all my PPE off, just to sit on the porch and have a homeowner watch me eat and make little remarks about my portion sizes or my weight. So yeah, I just tell them I eat in my truck or that I have a strict schedule to keep. And man, people think drywall repair is so easy, like you just buy a little pink tub of spackle and smear it on with a putty knife. But you can't do that on a big hole. You have to cut the drywall out square, put in wood backing strips, and use actual joint tape. I always prefer paper tape over the fiberglass mesh, because the mesh can crack on you if you don't use a hot mud—like a setting-type compound that cures chemically instead of just drying out. \n\nAnd then the most important part is you have to feather it out. You need a six-inch taping knife to bed the tape, then a ten-inch for the fill coat, and then a twelve-inch knife to really blend it into the rest of the wall. If you don't feather it wide enough, the second you put a coat of eggshell or satin paint on there and the hall light hits it, you're gonna see this massive, ugly hump in the wall. It drives me crazy when people just glob premixed joint compound on there and think they can sand it flat with a little sponge. You need a pole sander, and you have to shine a raking light across the wall to actually check your work before you even think about priming it. \n\nBut anyway, yeah, she wanted to do this whole big family dinner thing while I looked at her wall, and I just made up an excuse not to go. I just avoid those situations, same as the client meals. I just do not want the situation to turn into people sitting around a table commenting on what I eat or how I look. It’s just easier to stay away.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would feel better about yourself if you gained a little weight?\n\nPatient: Gained a little weight? No. No, man, absolutely not. If the scale goes up even a little bit, like if I do end up at a client dinner or eat something with bread, I get incredibly tense. \n\nActually, a lot of those client dinners happen right in the middle of kitchen remodels. And man, those exterior brick jobs are exhausting. People don't realize you can't just slap regular exterior latex on raw brick. The alkalinity in the masonry will literally burn the tint right out of the paint in six months. You have to pressure wash it first, let it dry completely, and then back-roll a heavy coat of masonry primer—something like Loxon—into every single mortar joint. You go through roller covers like crazy because the brick just shreds them. A three-quarter-inch nap is the bare minimum, and even then you're constantly jamming the brush in there to fill the pinholes. \n\nAnd getting the proportions right on a two-story wall is a whole other nightmare. I usually have to rent a tow-behind boom lift, wait until it's pitch black outside, and shine a high-lumen projector from across the street just to trace the outline. If you mess up the grid or the angle of the projector is off by even a few degrees, the whole image gets warped. \n\nSo you put all this blood, sweat, and tears into it for weeks... and then the business owner comes out and wants to take a picture of you standing next to the finished piece for their social media. And honestly? When I look at those photos, or if I just catch my reflection in the storefront glass while I'm loading the lift back onto the trailer, I'm not even looking at the artwork I just spent weeks on. I basically judge the whole day by whether my stomach and face look sharp enough in that moment. It just completely takes over my head, even when I'm supposed to be celebrating a finished job.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find it difficult to stop thinking about your weight, even when you're trying to focus on something else?\n\nPatient: Yeah, I mean, it's pretty much what I just said, honestly. Otherwise, the paint just peels off in big sheets a year later. \n\nAnd the masking for exterior spray jobs is a nightmare. You have to use special tape that sticks to masonry but won't pull the paint off the window frames, and you have to drape plastic over everything—cars, landscaping, the sidewalk. If the wind picks up even a little bit, overspray can drift for blocks. I had a buddy who sprayed a building on a slightly breezy day, and he ended up having to pay to detail like fifteen cars parked down the street because they all had tiny specks of gray paint on them. You have to use a low-pressure spray tip, keep the gun exactly twelve inches from the wall, and overlap your passes by fifty percent. Yeah, definitely. I know I sound like a broken record here, but it's exactly what I've been saying about catching myself in a mirror or looking at those photos next to my murals. It has absolutely nothing to do with the job I'm working on, but I'll still judge my whole day by whether my stomach and face look sharp enough in that moment. 

Like, I could be right in the middle of a massive interior job. You know, when a client wants to go from a dark navy blue or a crimson red to a stark white? People think paint is just magic. It's really not. If you don't use a high-hide primer—usually something tinted slightly gray, actually, because gray covers dark colors way better than white does—you're going to be putting on four coats of expensive topcoat. And even then, the dark color will flash through under certain lighting. And you have to use a 3/8-inch nap microfiber roller, because if you use a half-inch, it leaves way too much stipple, and the wall ends up looking like an orange peel. 

And don't even get me started on drywall dust. If the drywall guys didn't wipe down the walls with a damp sponge after sanding the mud, your primer is just going to stick to the dust, not the paper. I've seen whole strips of paint just peel right off the wall and wrap around the roller because of drywall dust. You have to use a PVA primer to seal the porous mud first, otherwise the finish coat flashes and looks completely dead and uneven in the spots where the joints are. 

But... yeah.
